choices: Choosing the action with the highest average payoff
Alternating actions in a fixed pattern
Randomizing over actions to keep rivals from predicting your move
Mixing two products in one market
explain: Slide p. 44. A fixed pattern is predictable, which defeats the purpose.

stem: When are mixed strategies most useful?
choices: When there is no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium
When both players have dominant strategies
In coordination games where both want to match
explain: Monitoring, penalty kicks, rock paper scissors: each side gains by being unpredictable.

stem: True or false: In a mixed strategy equilibrium, each player randomizes so that the OTHER player is indifferent between his or her actions.
explain: True. If the other player strictly preferred one action, you could be exploited.

stem: Which slide example is a game with no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium?
explain: The others each have a pure equilibrium.

stem: True or false: The mixed strategy formulas are printed on the equation sheet.
explain: False. Set up the expected payoffs and solve.

stem: In the Princess Bride scene, why should Westley not always poison the same cup?
choices: Poison only works in one cup
If Vizzini could predict it, he would drink from the safe cup
The game has a pure Nash equilibrium
explain: Predictability is exploited in a game with no pure equilibrium.

stem:
Boss (rows) and Employee (columns):

| Boss \ Employee | Work | Shirk |
|---|---|---|
| Monitor | 6, 3 | 8, 0 |
| Don't Monitor | 10, 3 | 2, 4 |

The boss monitors with probability p. What value of p makes the employee indifferent between working and shirking?
explain: Employee's payoff from Work: 3p + 3(1 - p) = 3. From Shirk: 0p + 4(1 - p) = 4 - 4p. Set equal: 3 = 4 - 4p, p = 0.25.

stem: Same game. The employee works with probability q. What value of q makes the boss indifferent between monitoring and not?
explain: Boss from Monitor: 6q + 8(1 - q) = 8 - 2q. From Don't: 10q + 2(1 - q) = 2 + 8q. Set equal: 6 = 10q, q = 0.6.

stem: Same game. In the mixed equilibrium (q = 0.6), what is the boss's expected payoff?

Employee monitoring from the slides:

| Boss \ Employee | Work | Shirk |
|---|---|---|
| Monitor | -1, 1 | 1, -1 |
| Don't Monitor | 1, -1 | -1, 1 |

With what probability should the boss monitor?
explain: Employee: Work = 1p - 1(1 - p) = 2p - 1; Shirk = -1p + 1(1 - p) = 1 - 2p. Equal when p = 0.5.

stem: A kicker shoots Left with probability p. The chance of scoring is 0.4 if kicker Left and goalie Left, 0.9 if Left/Right, 0.8 if Right/Left, 0.3 if Right/Right. What p makes the goalie indifferent between diving Left and Right?
explain: Goalie Left: scoring = 0.4p + 0.8(1 - p) = 0.8 - 0.4p. Goalie Right: 0.9p + 0.3(1 - p) = 0.3 + 0.6p. Equal: 0.5 = p.

stem: A tax agency audits some returns at random rather than following a published rule. Which concept explains this?
choices: A mixed strategy keeps taxpayers from predicting audits
explain: A predictable rule would let cheaters avoid it, like the monitoring game.

stem: In a mixed strategy equilibrium, the boss's monitoring probability is determined by:
explain: It must make the employee indifferent, so it is pinned down by the employee's payoffs.

stem: A boss monitors 60% of the time. At that rate the employee strictly prefers to work. Is the boss using the equilibrium mix?
choices: Yes; any mix is an equilibrium
No; the boss should always monitor
No; in equilibrium the employee is indifferent, so the boss could monitor less and save cost
explain: If the employee strictly prefers working, the boss is monitoring more than needed.
